newsitem.title: USA: IMF says Russia 1997 deal stresses reform, taxes.
newsitem.headline: IMF says Russia 1997 deal stresses reform, taxes.

text.p: A new 1997 program drawn up between Russia and the International Monetary Fund stresses the need to accelerate structural reforms and try to bring revenues under control, a senior IMF official said on Friday.
But John Odling-Smee, director of the IMF department dealing with Russia, told a seminar that the reformers in the new Russian government faced major problems.
Referring to massive tax arrears and huge fiscal problems, he said: "The government is clearly attempting to move faster on economic reforms and we at the IMF are very excited about that."
"We are well aware of the huge obstacles to reforms in Russia and hope they will have all the support they can get."

Members of the new government, including reformist First Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly Chubais, are due to attend part of the IMF spring meeting, although Chubais has said he does not plan to discuss Russia's IMF loan or the 1997 programme.

Odling-Smee, echoing comments from IMF Managing Director Michel Camdessus, said the IMF board would meet in May to consider the 1997 program, which stressed the need to take steps "to try to bring the revenue situation under control".
The IMF delayed several monthly payments on a three-year $10 billion loan to Russia because of low tax revenues.
"The implication of this is crucial and it is something the fund is much concerned about," Odling-Smee said.
Alexei Mozhin, Russia's Executive Director at the IMF, told the seminar that the new government team consisted of "the best people that Russia can offer".
"It is more coherent than any previous government team and that's why you can speak about prospects for a real turnaround," he said.
"But the risks and challenges facing this new team are really formidable -- the question is, if they fail, what happens next?" he said.
